_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship / standard romanization, give the basis in note), 'provisional' (romanization mine, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. 'pinyin' holds the romaji reading (this is a Japanese book). Flag main cast with "principal": true (+ optional "cast" one-liner, "cast_order") for the Principal Characters page.

土方歳三.cast: The novel's hero. A well-off farmer's son of Ishida village in the Tama country west of Edo, who becomes vice-commander of the Shinsengumi.
土方歳三.note: Historical figure, 1835–1869. Japanese name order, surname (Hijikata) first; the given name Toshizō carries a long final vowel. Called Toshi by his intimates.

近藤勇.cast: Toshizō's boyhood friend and sword-brother, from the neighboring village of Kamiishiwara; commander of the Shinsengumi.
近藤勇.note: Historical figure, 1834–1868. Head of the Tennen Rishin-ryū school of swordsmanship and, later, commander of the Shinsengumi.

佐藤彦五郎.note: Historical, 1827–1902. Headman (nanushi) of Hino, married to Toshizō's elder sister; his household kept the Tennen Rishin-ryū training hall where Kondō and Toshizō trained.

小桜.note: A bell-shaking shrine maiden (miko) at the Ōkunitama Shrine in Fuchū; a minor character. Romanization mine.

お佐絵.note: Younger sister of the Saruwatari chief priest of Fuchū; the woman Toshizō meets in the festival dark. Apparently the novelist's invention. Romanization mine.

猿渡.note: The hereditary house of chief priests (gūji) of the Ōkunitama Shrine at Fuchū, documented from the fourteenth century.

梶川景次.note: A master of the Shintō Munen-ryū with a training hall at Sakuramachi in Kōfu; a minor figure. Reading of the given name uncertain; romanization mine.

六車宗伯.note: A swordsman of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, deputy master at Fuchū, whom Toshizō kills in this chapter. The surname is read Rokusha on the source’s own furigana (ろくしゃそうはく), echoing the Rokusha Myōjin shrine he serves; hence the chapter title, ‘Cutting Down Rokusha.’

瀬木掃部.note: One of the hereditary priestly houses (shake) of the Rokusha Myōjin at Fuchū, in whose residence Rokusha Sōhaku lodged. Romanization mine.

松平伊織.note: A hatamoto of eight hundred koku with a residence in Honjo, Edo; Osae’s late husband, married to her when she was seventeen. A minor figure; reading from the source’s furigana.

近藤内蔵助.note: A rōnin of Enshū, late-eighteenth-century founder of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

近藤周斎.note: Historical. Third head of the Tennen Rishin-ryū (personal name Shūsuke; in retirement, Shūsai), who adopted the farm boy Katsuta and made him Kondō Isami, his heir.

井上源三郎.cast: A steady older man of the Tama circle, from Hino, a Tennen Rishin-ryū fencer who follows Kondō to Kyoto and captains the Shinsengumi's Sixth Unit.
井上源三郎.note: Historical, 1829–1868. One of the founding Tama members of the Shinsengumi; killed at Toba-Fushimi.

永倉新八.cast: A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, a rōnin of Matsumae and one of the corps' great swordsmen; later captain of the Shinsengumi's Second Unit.
永倉新八.note: Historical, 1839–1915. Held the full transmission of the Shintō Munen-ryū; survived the Restoration and left an inside memoir of the corps.

藤堂平助.note: Historical, 1844–1867. A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū; later captain of the Shinsengumi’s Eighth Unit, killed at the Aburanokōji affair after joining Itō Kashitarō’s breakaway.

七里研之助.cast: A fair-skinned iai master with a mark below his right eye, deputy at the Hiruma hall; Toshizō's recurring nemesis, who hunts him for the killing of Rokusha.
七里研之助.note: The chief personal antagonist of the novel's early and middle chapters. An iai master of the Araki-ryū, trained first in the Maniwa Nen-ryū; reading from the source's furigana (しちりけんのすけ).

沖田総司.cast: A boyish prodigy of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, raised at Kondō's Edo hall; the corps's finest swordsman, later captain of the First Unit.
沖田総司.note: Historical, about 1842–1868. Died young of consumption; one of the most beloved figures of the Shinsengumi legend.

お咲.note: A meshimori-onna at the Jōshūya inn in Fuda, a thin-lipped Jōshū woman; a minor figure. Romanization mine.

理兵衛.note: Keeper of the Jōshūya inn at Fuda, the Tennen Rishin-ryū men's regular lodging. Romanization mine.

善海.note: Abbot of the Senjubō, the Shinshū temple in Hachiōji where Toshizō lodged in his peddling days. Romanization mine.

大島新五右衛門.note: An eighteenth-century rural samurai of Kōzuke (died 1779) famous for a trick-drawing feat of the Araki-ryū iai.

半造.note: Son of Hiruma Yohachi and head, from a hall in Senninmachi at Hachiōji, of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū; married to Sen, daughter of the abbot of the Senjubō.

辰吉.note: A young man of Renjaku who peddled horse-sandals at Hachiōji; a passing figure.

石翠.note: Toshizō's eldest brother, blind from birth, who gave up the succession and lived by his arts — a shrewd, polished man. A historical figure (the eldest Hijikata brother); Sekisui is his elegant by-name.

喜六.note: A farmer of Ishida village, Toshizō's eldest surviving brother and head of the house.

千葉栄次郎.note: Historical, 1833–1862. Second son of Chiba Shūsaku and a swordsman prodigy of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, nicknamed the Little Tengu of Chiba.

周作.note: Founder of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and of the Genbukan hall in Edo; father of Eijirō. One of the great sword-reformers of the age.

岡田総右衛門.note: Founder of the Ryūgō-ryū of Warabi, the shin-cutting country school.

権.note: An old temple servant of the Shōkōin, once rescued by Toshizō, who serves as his scout. Romanization from the source's furigana.

おのぶ.note: Toshizō's elder sister, wife of Satō Hikogorō.

新田義貞.note: The fourteenth-century commander who, for the emperor Go-Daigo, destroyed the Kamakura shogunate; victor at Bubaigawara in 1333.

三浦義勝.note: A Sagami warrior whose reinforcements turned the Battle of Bubaigawara for Nitta.

真庭十郎左衛門.note: As Shiba gives him, the head of the Nen-ryū house at Maniwa and Chiba Shūsaku's antagonist in the Ikaho affair. The historical head of the Maniwa Nen-ryū was of the Higuchi family; Shiba names him from the school's seat.

深津.note: A pupil of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, set to make fire during the ambush; a passing figure.

桂小五郎.cast: A Chōshū swordsman, head student of the Renpeikan, blessed in birth, learning, and skill; later, as Kido Takayoshi, an architect of the Meiji Restoration. Toshizō's opposite in every advantage.
桂小五郎.note: Historical, 1833–1877. Later known as Kido Takayoshi, one of the leaders of the Restoration.

原田左之助.cast: A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, a hot-blooded spearman of Iyo; later a captain of the Shinsengumi.
原田左之助.note: Historical, 1840–1868. A spearman of the Hōzōin line; died in the fighting around Edo.

坂本竜馬.note: Historical, 1836–1867. Of Tosa, a Hokushin Ittō-ryū swordsman of the Chiba hall; later the great broker of the Restoration, assassinated in 1867.

斎藤弥九郎.note: Master of the Renpeikan, the Shintō Munen-ryū hall reckoned one of the three great dōjō of Edo; Kondō's source of borrowed swordsmen.

桃井春蔵.note: Master of the Shigakukan, one of the three great dōjō of Edo. Reading from the source's furigana (もものい).

塚原卜伝.note: A sword-saint of the sixteenth century.

伊藤一刀斎.note: Founder of the Ittō-ryū line of swordsmanship.

宮本武蔵.note: The famous seventeenth-century duelist, author of The Book of Five Rings.

おつね.note: Kondō Isami's wife, a silent, gloomy woman and, by Toshizō's account, a poor cook.

楠正成.note: The fourteenth-century loyalist commander, byword for cunning generalship against the odds; claimed founder of the Kusunoki school of military science.

武田信玄.note: The sixteenth-century warlord of Kai, whose tactics were handed down as the Kōshū school of military science.

江川.note: The hereditary intendant house at Nirayama, administering shogunal land.

山南敬助.cast: The eldest of the Shieikan house-guests, a learned Sendai man and Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept; brings the corps its political news. Toshizō despises him.
山南敬助.note: Historical, 1833–1865. Held the full transmission at the Chiba hall; later general secretary (sōchō) of the Shinsengumi, second only to Kondō, until an attempt to leave the corps forced him to commit seppuku.

芹沢鴨.cast: A huge, violent Mito rōnin of the Shintō Munen-ryū, of the Tengu Party; co-commander of the founding Mibu corps, and Toshizō's uneasy first ally in Kyoto.
芹沢鴨.note: Historical, 1826/27–1863. A Mito man of the Shindō Munen-ryū, real name given variously as Kimura or Shimomura Tsuguji; first head of the Mibu corps, assassinated by the Kondō faction in the ninth month of 1863.

斎藤一.cast: A close, taciturn swordsman, a rōnin of Akashi who joins the corps from the Shieikan; one of its finest blades.
斎藤一.note: Historical, 1844–1915. Later captain of the Shinsengumi's Third Unit and one of its deadliest swordsmen; survived the wars, served as a Meiji policeman, and died in old age.

清河八郎.note: Historical, 1830–1863. A rural samurai of Shōnai in Dewa, a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept and strategist; conceived the Rōshigumi and tried to turn it to the imperial cause, and was cut down for it in 1863.

松平上総介.note: As Shiba gives him: a collateral Tokugawa, of the line of Tadanaga, acting as a sponsor of the rōshi levy. A minor figure; reading of the title as the source gives it.

松平忠敏.note: A Kōbusho instructor placed in charge of the shogunate's rōshi levy of 1863. Reading from the source's furigana (ただとし).

山岡鉄太郎.note: Historical, 1836–1888. A shogunal overseer of the Rōshigumi; later famous as Yamaoka Tesshū, a great swordsman, statesman, and Zen adept who helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle.

松平容保.note: Historical, 1836–1893. Lord of Aizu and, from 1862, Kyoto Protector (Kyoto Shugoshoku); under his patronage the Mibu corps became the Shinsengumi.

板倉周防守.note: Itakura Katsukiyo (1823–1889), a senior councilor (rōjū) of the shogunate.

新見錦.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction and an early officer of the corps; forced to commit seppuku in 1863. Reading from the source's furigana (にいみにしき).

平間重助.note: A Mito follower and inner pupil of Serizawa Kamo. Romanization mine.

野口健司.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction and an early Shinsengumi officer; died in 1864.

平山五郎.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction, killed alongside Serizawa in the assassination of 1863.

石坂周造.note: A defector from Hikone and follower of Kiyokawa; survived into the mid-Meiji years as a man of business, remembered as a pioneer of the Japanese petroleum trade.

池田徳太郎.note: A Geishū (Hiroshima) rōnin of the Kiyokawa faction, active in the levying of the Rōshigumi.

根岸友山.note: A wealthy Musashi headman and expel-the-barbarian sympathizer who enrolled in the Rōshigumi with a following of his own.

八木源之丞.note: A rural samurai of Mibu whose house lodged the corps; the Yagi residence survives as a site of Shinsengumi history.

頼山陽.note: Historical, 1780–1832. Confucian historian and poet, author of the Nihon Gaishi, whose romantic, imperial-centered narrative of Japanese history deeply shaped late-shogunate loyalism.

孝明天皇.note: Reigned 1846–1867. Fiercely opposed to opening the country to foreigners, he lent the loyalist cause an imperial sanction the shogunate could not command.

石田村.note: Toshizō's birthplace in the Tama district of Musashi; now part of Hino, Tokyo.

武州多摩.note: The Tama district of Musashi Province (Bushū), the farming country west of Edo; the Shinsengumi's home ground.

府中.note: The old provincial seat of Musashi, on the Kōshū Highway; site of the Ōkunitama Shrine.

八王子.note: A town west of Fuchū on the Kōshū Highway.

甲州街道.note: One of the five great Tokugawa highways, running west from Edo through Fuchū toward Kōfu in Kai (Kōshū).

大国魂神社.note: The head shrine (sōja) of Musashi Province, at Fuchū; also called the Rokusha Myōjin or Rokusho-gū. Its grand festival is the Kurayami (Darkness) Festival.

専修坊.note: The Shinshū temple in Hachiōji of the winter episode. Reading from the source's own furigana; romanization mine.

蕨.note: A post-town just north of Edo, in present-day Saitama; base of the Ryūgō-ryū.

秩父.note: The hill country of western Musashi; home ground of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū.

本所.note: A district on the east bank of the Sumida in Edo.

小石川小日向柳町.note: The Edo neighborhood where Kondō’s training hall (the Shieikan) stood.

上州屋.note: Rihei's inn at the Fuda station on the Kōshū Highway.

布田.note: The central station of the Fuda Five Stations on the Kōshū Highway, in present-day Chōfu.

内藤新宿.note: The first post-station out of Edo on the Kōshū Highway.

上石原.note: A village of the Fuda Five Stations on the Kōshū Highway (now part of Chōfu); Kondō Isami's birthplace.

連雀.note: A village of the Tama country with no fencing hall, where Toshizō taught in the headman's miso storehouse.

小仏峠.note: The pass west of Hachiōji by which the Kōshū Highway crosses into Kai.

千人町.note: The Hachiōji quarter named for the Thousand Guardsmen settled there; site of the Hiruma hall.

馬庭.note: The seat of the Maniwa Nen-ryū in Kōzuke (Jōshū), present-day Gunma.

分倍河原.note: A district on the old Tama-River flats near Fuchū, a road-junction long fought over; site of the 1333 battle and of the duel of this chapter.

分倍橋.note: A small bridge south of Bubaigawara, the appointed place of the fight.

正光院.note: A field-temple with a graveyard near Bubaigawara, where Toshizō sets up his command post.

韮山.note: A seat in Izu of the Egawa house, hereditary shogunal intendants.

伊香保.note: A hot-spring town in Kōzuke (Jōshū), site of the shrine tablet affair between Chiba Shūsaku and the Nen-ryū.

長州.note: The Mōri domain of western Honshū, later the chief power of the anti-shogunal movement and the Shinsengumi's great enemy.

玄武館.note: Chiba Shūsaku's Hokushin Ittō-ryū hall in Edo, greatest of the three great dōjō.

三番町.note: An Edo quarter to which the Saitō hall (Renpeikan) moved after a fire.

壬生.note: A village in the western outskirts of Kyoto, the first quarters and base of the corps that became the Shinsengumi (called, in derision, the Mibu-rō, the ‘Mibu wolves’).

新徳寺.note: The temple at Mibu that served as the Rōshigumi's headquarters, where Kiyokawa revealed his true design.

中仙道.note: The inland highway between Edo and Kyoto, running through the central mountains; longer than the coastal Tōkaidō but free of its river-crossings.

会津.note: The Matsudaira domain of the mountainous northeast, staunchly loyal to the shogunate; its lord was Kyoto Protector and the Shinsengumi's patron, and it fought the Restoration to a bitter end in 1868.

水戸.note: A senior Tokugawa branch domain, and the intellectual seedbed of the revere-the-Emperor school; riven in these years by violent factional strife between its radicals (the Tengu Party) and conservatives.

新選組.note: The 'Newly Selected Corps,' the shogunate's Kyoto police militia of swordsmen, 1863–1869; the subject of the novel.

天然理心流.note: The country school of swordsmanship, founded by Kondō Kuranosuke and headed in this book by Kondō Isami; the school of Hijikata, Okita, and the Tama men. Known for overwhelming an opponent’s spirit and for close, practical fighting rather than polish.

甲源一刀流.note: A sword school of the Chichibu country, founded 1776 by Henmi Tashirō; the school of Rokusha Sōhaku and, along the Kōshū Highway, the chief rival of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

柳剛流.note: A school founded by Okada Sōemon, based at Warabi, notorious for shin-cutting strikes and for teaching the glaive alongside the sword.

北辰一刀流.note: The great Edo sword school of Chiba Shūsaku, at the height of its fame in these years; Tōdō Heisuke’s school.

神道無念流.note: A widely practiced Edo sword school; Nagakura Shinpachi held its full transmission.

荒木流.note: A composite martial school of Kōzuke, taught iai among other arts; Shichiri Kennosuke's iai line.

念流.note: Here the Maniwa Nen-ryū of Kōzuke, one of the oldest surviving sword schools; where Shichiri first trained.

浪士組.note: The ‘corps of masterless men,’ levied by the shogunate in 1863 to go up to Kyoto ostensibly as the shogun's guard. Split by Kiyokawa's imperial gambit; the remnant that stayed in Kyoto became the Shinsengumi.

天狗党.note: The radical revere-the-Emperor faction of the Mito domain, which in 1864 rose in open revolt and was crushed.

京都守護職.note: The shogunal office created in 1862 to keep order in Kyoto, held by Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu; the Shinsengumi served under its authority.

石田散薬.note: The Hijikata family's patent remedy for bruises and broken bones, made and peddled from the early eighteenth century until 1948.

里.note: A unit of distance, about 3.9 km (2.4 miles).

名主.note: The headman of a village, lowest office of Tokugawa rural administration: a leading farmer, not a samurai.

旗本.note: A direct bannerman of the shogun, with the right of audience; a samurai of the Tokugawa house itself, ranked above the ordinary domain retainer.

居合.note: The art of drawing the sword and cutting in a single motion; a specialty distinct from ordinary fencing.

代官.note: A shogunal officer administering a district of the Tokugawa house's own lands in place of a resident lord.

衢地.note: From Sunzi's Art of War: a place where the roads of several regions meet, from which armies are readily moved.

気組.note: The marshalling of spirit to overwhelm an opponent; the watchword of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

太平記.note: The fourteenth-century war-chronicle of the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts, a storytellers' staple.

猿田彦.note: The guiding deity of Japanese myth, shown as a long-nosed, red-faced figure; his mask (rubied here in the source as Sarudahiko) was one of those the waiwai-tennō wore.

牛頭天王.note: The 'Ox-Head Heavenly King,' plague-warding deity of the Gion and Tennō shrines, whose talismans the waiwai-tennō sold.

尊皇攘夷.note: The rallying slogan of the late-shogunate loyalists: reverence for the Emperor joined to the demand that the foreigner be driven out. Its logic pointed, in the end, past the shogunate itself.

講武所.note: The shogunate's own military academy in Edo, opened in 1856 to modernize the training of its retainers in swordsmanship, gunnery, and Western arms.

辻斬り.note: ‘Crossroads-cutting’: the testing of a blade, or of one's nerve, by cutting down a stranger on the road at night. Long a capital crime, it revived in the murderous mood of these years.

鉄扇.note: A folding fan with iron ribs (or a solid iron bar shaped like one), carried where a sword might give offense and used to parry or strike.

公用方.note: A domain's political-liaison bureau, handling its dealings with the court, the shogunate, and other domains in Kyoto.

和泉守兼定.note: A celebrated sword-signature. The blade Hijikata carried through his life bore it; see the note at its first appearance.

虎徹.note: The prized blades of the Edo smith Nagasone Kotetsu. Kondō's famous ‘Kotetsu’ was, by most accounts, a forgery; see the note where he hunts for one.
